Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

🚨 🇮🇳INDIA IS MAKING SIM BINDING MANDATORY, NO ACTIVE SIM, NO WHATSAPP OR TELEGRAM?

Starting January 1, 2027, messaging apps using Indian mobile numbers will face new SIM-binding requirements under the government’s directive.

Here’s what changes 👇

WHAT IS SIM BINDING?

Currently, you can verify WhatsApp using an OTP and continue using it even after removing the SIM.

Under SIM binding, the app must remain linked to the active SIM associated with your registered number, installed in your phone.

Remove or deactivate that SIM, and the app may stop working until it is restored and verified.

WHICH APPS ARE AFFECTED?

WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, ShareChat, JioChat, Arattai and Josh are among the apps covered by the directive.

WHY IS INDIA DOING THIS?

The government says scammers exploit messaging accounts that keep working without their registered SIM. This can help fraudsters operate remotely, impersonate officials, run phishing attacks and carry out digital arrest and investment scams.

The aim is to improve traceability and make such fraud harder.

WHAT ARE THE CONCERNS?

-> People using Wi-Fi-only devices or multiple devices could face access issues.
-> Users may face inconvenience when changing or replacing SIM cards.
-> Privacy, implementation and the effectiveness of the rule remain concerns.

The government has extended the compliance deadline to December 31, 2026, with the new requirements set to apply from January 1, 2027.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu condemns arbitrary content and account restrictions faced by users on Meta platforms, X, and Reddit.

Over the past 20 days, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu’s Free Speech Tracker has recorded 200+ cases of content blocking and account restrictions on @Meta platforms, @X, and @Reddit. Many of the recently blocked posts were critical of the government, called for protests, featured journalists’ reporting, addressed ongoing issues, or even demanded justice in a murder case, among other topics. These restrictions are not only limited to feed posts, but Meta has also restricted Instagram Stories and comments online. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has also recorded various instances of FIRs filed against users raising their voices online.

Those affected include stand-up comedians, journalists, digital media organisations, civil society organisations, cartoonists, meme pages, political representatives and other users. Out of these, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has recorded 20+ independent journalists and digital media organisations who have faced restrictions, including @LiveLawIndia, @moliticsindia, and @4pmnews_network.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the platforms or through Meta’s automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight.

In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making.

These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI-generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless.

text:
#PressCoverage #BriarApp

@arjunadriandsa, Senior Legal Counsel, https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu has recently been featured in an article by @moneycontrolcom. The story talks about the recent Delhi High Court order regarding the blocking of the Briar app.

Arjun who represented Briar in court said “Earlier, in most cases, blocking orders have been furnished to the court under sealed cover, which is very opaque. The Supreme Court in itself has said the same in the Madhyamam case (ban on Media One). Even if the government is furnishing a blocking order under sealed cover, then the non-disclosure of reasons should be proved through cogent material. Department issued notice U/s. 73 but confirmed demand U/s. 74 without any fraud allegations to block amnesty: Madras HC quashes order, restoring Assessee’s right to relief U/s. 128A.

Issue:
Whether the Department can convert proceedings initiated U/s. 73 into an assessment order U/s. 74 without alleging fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression, thereby disqualifying the Assessee from amnesty U/s. 128A.

Rule:
Sections 73 and 74 draw a clear boundary, as Section 74 strictly requires proof of fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts with intent to evade tax. By virtue of Section 75(2), where allegations of fraud are not established, the proceedings must be treated and determined strictly U/s. 73, which in turn permits an eligible taxpayer to seek statutory waiver of interest and penalty U/s. 128A.

Application:
The Department issued a show cause notice on 29.09.2023 U/s. 73 for a mere ITC difference between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A, raising no charge of fraudulent intent. However, the Department passed an assessment order on 08.12.2023 confirming the tax U/s. 74 along with a 100% penalty, which subsequently led to the rejection of the Assessee's waiver plea U/s. 128A on 06.01.2026. The High Court observed that a routine ITC discrepancy does not amount to deliberate tax evasion, and since neither the notice nor the order established the essential ingredients of fraud or wilful suppression, the Department could not have invoked Section 74, making Section 75(2) squarely applicable to mandate adjudication only U/s. 73.

Conclusion:
The High Court quashed both the Section 74 assessment order and the rejection order, remanded the case back to the Department to pass a fresh order strictly U/s. 73, and granted liberty to the Assessee to file a fresh application for waiver U/s. 128A within the prescribed statutory period.

Impact Analysis:
The ruling prevents the Department from arbitrarily converting routine Section 73 notices into Section 74 orders to deny an Assessee the statutory benefit of penalty and interest waiver under Section 128A.

Deepfake technology is advancing rapidly. AI-generated videos can imitate a person's face, expressions and voice so convincingly that spotting the manipulation with the naked eye can be difficult.

But technology is also being developed to detect these fabrications. Maharashtra Cyber has highlighted tools designed to analyse suspected deepfakes and provide technical assessments, reportedly within seconds in some cases. The exact detection time and availability of an official certificate may depend on the tool and the case.

This matters because a fake video can damage reputations, spread misinformation and be used for impersonation, fraud or blackmail before the truth catches up.

If a suspicious video targets you or someone you know, don't panic and don't amplify it by forwarding it further. Preserve the original link and relevant evidence, and seek verification through appropriate official channels.

If the incident involves financial cyber fraud in India, call 1930 immediately. For other cybercrime complaints, use the official portal at https://t.co/K5hILpknes.

Remember, no single detection tool is infallible. Independent verification and timely reporting remain essential.

Don't let a convincing fake become your accepted truth. Verify first. Share later.

text:
INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

if you are using Claude Code to build apps, check this simple but important tip:

let's say 𝘊𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘥𝘦 𝘊𝘰𝘥𝘦 created 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘤𝘬𝘰𝘶t page, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘥𝘦, ran them, and they all pass!

think about it! a test is just code that checks other code, and here the same session wrote both. 

so if it guessed wrong in the code, it guessed wrong in the tests too, and green only means 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳!

so when you tested it, you saw "12" tests and "12" green checks, and you tested and paid with your own card, and everything worked!

now Claude keeps building all week, and it adds 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘆:

"12 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘰𝘯 𝘔𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘢𝘺... 40 𝘣𝘺 𝘞𝘦𝘥𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘥𝘢𝘺... 120 𝘣𝘺 𝘍𝘳𝘪𝘥𝘢𝘺, 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘯"

that's 𝟭𝟮𝟬 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀, and not one of them tries a declined card: Claude assumed every card goes through, so the code and the tests both skip it. more tests won't save you, each new one copies the same guess. 

meanwhile, a customer whose card was declined just got their order for free!! 

𝘀𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁?

let's learn about "𝙩𝙚𝙨𝙩𝙨 𝙛𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙨𝙥𝙚𝙘"

the idea is simple:

write down what the checkout must do before the code exists (that's the spec), and let the tests come from that list, not from the code.

• the spec: a few plain lines, like "a declined card makes no order" and "an order over $50 ships free"
• the tests: a fresh session that never saw the code turns each line into a test
• the check: run the tests against the code. a red test means the code or the spec is wrong, and you decide which

tests come in three layers
- small to big: unit (one function, like the free shipping math)
- integration (the pieces together: your database, the payment service)
- end-to-end (a real click through checkout). use the smallest layer that proves the line.

careful: "all tests pass" isn't "the product works". a case nobody wrote down never gets tested, so read the spec yourself before Claude builds: it's the one part only you can get right.

ask Claude:
"write a short spec for my checkout as plain lines of what must happen and show it to me first, then have a separate sub-agent write unit, integration and end-to-end tests from that spec only, without reading how you built it, run them, and tell me which lines fail."

you don't have to write this code yourself. you just have to know 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰 exists, 𝘀𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽.

this is block 𝟲𝟬 of 𝗩𝗶𝗯𝗲 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝘀.

A simple "I accept" checkbox won't save you under the DPDP Act. 

Most platforms treat consent like a formality, but DPDP changes the rules:

- Purpose Limitation: Blanket consent is out. Purpose must be specific and explicit.
- Defined Timelines: No indefinite data holding. You must state the exact duration.
- Right to Withdraw & Erase: If a user withdraws consent or asks for data erasure, processing must stop, and data must be purged immediately.

A basic cookie banner is only 1% of compliance. Real consent management requires full lifecycle governance.

@Meta is becoming a serious threat to India's democracy, digital sovereignty, and potentially even electoral integrity.

It's a treason 😡

Every single day, hundreds of Instagram accounts are allegedly being restricted, suspended or permanently removed in India without meaningful notice, transparency, independent review or due process. This is a fundamental violation of the principles of natural justice.

No proper hearing. No reasoned order. No effective appeal. No accountability.

And this absence of due process has created something even more disturbing: an underground ransom market for account restoration.

People are allegedly negotiating with creators and demanding money in dollars to restore suspended accounts. I have screenshots of such negotiations. Imagine a system where an account can disappear overnight, its owner cannot obtain a fair hearing, and shady intermediaries suddenly appear offering restoration for money!

Meanwhile, thousands of small content creators risk losing their livelihoods. Years of work, audiences, professional credibility and income can disappear because of an opaque automated decision.

Even more alarming is the apparent misuse or overbroad application of India's IT Rules.

I have evidence of completely ordinary content, including simple sports discussions with no apparent connection to politics, government criticism or unlawful activity, being restricted in India through systems citing Indian legal requirements.

How does an ordinary sports discussion become a threat requiring restriction in India? Who issued the instruction? Under which provision? Where is the reasoned order?

These questions deserve answers.

The consequences are particularly devastating for small creators and independent journalists. Established media organisations have legal teams, institutional resources and political connections. Independent journalists and emerging creators have none of these protections.

And this is precisely why the situation is so dangerous.

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics recognised research explaining how innovation and "creative destruction" challenge established economic structures. New entrants threaten incumbents by introducing new ideas, technologies and competition.

The same principle has a powerful democratic parallel.

New journalists challenge established media monopolies. Independent creators challenge controlled narratives. Citizen journalists challenge institutional gatekeeping.

When emerging voices are disproportionately silenced, the result is not merely content moderation. It risks protecting the existing information monopoly from democratic competition.

A government does not need to shut down every newspaper or arrest every journalist to suppress dissent. If independent voices can be systematically restricted before they become influential, the next generation of critical journalism can be strangled at birth.

This is how digital authoritarianism can operate without formally declaring censorship.

And the biggest concern goes far beyond digital sovereignty.

A foreign private corporation controlling the visibility, distribution and survival of political speech has enormous potential influence over public opinion.

If political criticism is disproportionately suppressed while favourable narratives remain amplified, electoral competition itself can be distorted.

Manipulation of political visibility can become manipulation of electoral choices. And interference with free and fair elections is an attack on the sovereignty of the Indian people themselves.

The Constitution derives its authority from "We, the People", not from Meta's algorithms, corporate executives or any ruling political party.

Yet where does an ordinary citizen seek justice when platform appeals are ineffective and even the independence and accountability of institutions such as the Election Commission and judiciary are being publicly questioned?  1/2

elon musk's grok bot found a hidden profile on my phone that recorded my screen, camera and location for 19 days. $12,400 was stolen from my bank account using 2FA codes screenshotted off my screen in real time. all from 20 minutes of charging at the airport

my flight was delayed. i sat down at gate B6 and plugged into the free USB port built into the armrest. 20 minutes. that's it

nothing happened. no popup. no notification. phone charged and i went home

two weeks later Chase calls me. suspicious wire transfer. $8,200 to an account i've never heard of. i open Zelle, two more. $2,400 on the 12th. $1,800 on the 17th. all three went through. all three had my 2FA codes

i couldn't figure out how. i have authenticator apps. i don't click links. i don't download random shit. my passwords are all unique

i plugged my iPhone into my MacBook and ran grok on the full device backup

the first thing it found made me put my phone down

a hidden MDM profile. mobile device management, the same system companies use to control work phones. remote camera. remote mic. screen recording. location tracking. full access to messages, photos, contacts, browser history. and a rogue root certificate that intercepted every HTTPS connection on my phone

it was called "AirPort Free Wi-Fi." it installed itself silently through the USB cable at the airport. no permission screen. no popup. nothing. just slid right in

server: https://t.co/ypwrOPtkKm
location: Chisinau, Moldova
domain age: 4 months
WHOIS: privacy-protected

19 days active. 847 commands executed on my phone. 612 location pings, one every 15 minutes. they mapped my apartment. my office. my daughter's school. my entire daily routine for almost three weeks

94 screenshots pulled from my phone. my Chase balance. my iMessage threads. my gmail password reset screens. my authenticator app with the codes on display. they didn't need to hack anything. they just watched my screen and used the codes before i could

4,291 photos exported. 1,247 contacts. 2,840 URLs from my browser history

the part that hit me the hardest was the location data. they had my daughter's school pinpointed by day 3. they knew what time i dropped her off and picked her up. every day for 19 days

$12,400. three transactions. all approved with 2FA codes they screenshotted off my phone in real time. by the time Chase flagged it the money was already in Moldova

i didn't get hacked by clicking a link. i didn't download malware. i plugged my phone into a USB port at an airport to charge it while i waited for my flight

what i did that night:

> removed the MDM profile and the rogue root certificate
> changed every password from my wife's laptop, not from my phone
> froze all cards, disputed all three transactions
> called the bank and put verbal verification on wire transfers
> filed a police report and an FTC complaint
> ordered a $12 USB data blocker off amazon. that's all it would have taken

my wife asked me why i was up at 3am. i showed her the grok output. she didn't say anything for about ten minutes. then she asked if they had photos of our daughter. they did. 4,291 of them

check your phone right now. settings > general > VPN & device management. if there is anything there you don't recognize, screenshot it and remove it immediately

don't ever plug your phone into a USB port you don't own. not at the airport. not at the hotel. not at the coffee shop. bring a wall adapter. bring a power bank. a USB cable is not just power. it's a data connection straight into your phone

the full scan takes 3 minutes. the prompt is in the comments. run it tonight on every phone in your house. send this to anyone you know who travels

text:
Ireland put the tweeter on trial, not the groper

I cannot believe the resources the state has mustered to go after a guy for making a tweet.

I'm writing this on the lunch break of Kirk Loco's trial in Bray, County Wicklow, about an hour south of Dublin. Kirk is being prosecuted for a tweet warning young women about migrant men harassing girls on a public bus. The tweet was true. And the man he warned about was in the courtroom today as the prosecution's main witness.

I can't identify him. He's a refugee claimant, and the lawyers and police warned me not to say anything that could reveal who he is. I'll say only that he needed an Arabic translator.

He testified he did nothing wrong, that he was just looking for a place to plug in his phone. Then he said his phone fell on the floor, which is why he got up and sat down next to the teenage girls. He never explained why he moved from the seat in front of them to the seat beside them, blocking the aisle.

According to the girl, he groped her, his belt was undone and his pants were so low his pubic hair was visible. She was so frightened she fled downstairs on the double-decker bus.

How do we know all this? There were about 10 CCTV cameras on that bus. They show him moving back and forth around the girl. They show that when the bus stopped and it was clear he was in trouble, he went to the back and played possum. Thirty-eight seconds from chatting to another passenger to out cold.

The driver testified he was obviously faking. Asked about that, he told the court: “I'm known as a very quick sleeper.”

I've been to 100 trials in my life, maybe more, and I don't think I've ever seen a shiftier witness. He took two or three positions on every question and switched mid-answer. I don't think the judge was buying it either.

Laoise de Brún, the barrister we're crowdfunding for Kirk, sliced and diced him on cross-examination. It was like shooting fish in a barrel.

Then a senior Garda took the stand and talked about the refugee accommodation at Newtownmountkennedy. He described the migrant men there as “vulnerable.”

Irish teenage girls are allegedly being harassed, and the men are the vulnerable ones?

He also described an incident where men from that centre were filming young girls at a sporting event. His response was to have them delete the videos — he deleted the evidence.

There's a term in psychology, DARVO: deny, attack, reverse victim and offender. That's what I watched today. The whole system is upside down. The hero of this story, according to the prosecution, is a man who admitted touching this girl and having his pants down. The villain is the man who warned the neighbourhood.

This is Kirk's 10th court appearance. He faces possible jail. The trial is only half over, and I'll have more from inside the courtroom.

If you want to help pay for Kirk's lawyers, and for Hugh Fagan, who goes on trial Tuesday, please go to https://t.co/SewO5oD5BL.

I don't think I'm easily shocked. I've seen too much. But I have never seen anything like this. Ireland needs help.

🚨 ALLEGED CON ARTIST: Who is Louise Lucas? 

Let me share with you the backstory on a self-described "greedy" lawmaker who waged a war on merit, denigrating Asian American parents and families, and is now indicted for illegally selling marijuana and cheating to create "generational wealth" 

The text that indicts Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas in a new Justice Department indictment announced by US Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel against her for alleged money laundering is this one:

💰 “this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

The words she allegedly later said: 
💰 “I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

Lucas is an important window into the choices that everyone faces: whether to advance in life through merit or through cheating. 

Read our coverage of the indictment here: 

'FOR PEOPLE WHO LOOK LIKE ME'
I know the day that I learned the name of Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas: Feb. 18, 2021. 

WATCH the video I've shared her to see Lucas in action.

She was supporting Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell and other Democratic lawmakers as they waged a wider battle to remove merit-based admissions to America's former No. 1 high school, Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, and other governor schools. Their bill: HB 2305.

There were some 20 mostly immigrant parents waiting to speak in the online waiting room: parents from India, China and elsewhere, who saw merit as the only path they have to realizing the American Dream and maybe if they were lucky creating "generational wealth."

Lucas wouldn't let the parents speak. I was watching the debate from the waiting room. My son was attending the school at the time, and I was writing about the efforts of parents to challenge the new admissions policy, eliminating the merit admissions test, as racist. 

A federal judge Conrad Hilton later supported the parents and the Coalition for TJ and called the new admissions policy "patently unconsitutional" and racist.

The ruling was overturned on appeal and the US Supreme Court wouldn't hear the appeal but is now set to hear a similar case from Montgomery County, Md.

Then-state Sen. Chap Petersen was opposing that effort as an effort to target the school's mostly Asian American student population. 

As Petersen spoke about TJ, he noted, “Its population is 80 percent minority.”

Lucas, who is black, interrupted him and said, “Sen. Petersen, for people who look like me, I would appreciate it if you would put a better definition to minority, because I know you’re not talking about people who look like me, so could you please, please be more specific?”

Petersen, whose wife is Korean American woman, said: “The population is about 70 percent Asian.”

Then he added: “People who look like my kids. My kids.” 

Lucas responded: "Mm-hmm."

The war on merit succeeded and TJHSST has plummeted in academic standards and national rankings and is now the FORMER No. 1 high school. Current Virginia Lt. Governor Ghazala Hashmi demonized "parents" and alleged they were racist and supported Lucas and Surovell. 

When Lucas lost the vote, she said: "We will overcome one day."

🔗 This is the full 2018 debate for anyone who wants to see Lucas and her war on merit: https://t.co/w7iGZqXnnW

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

China's Ministry of Public Security has been running informal "police stations" inside the United States. Not metaphorically. Actual proxy-operated stations conducting surveillance and coercion of Chinese nationals on American soil. The CECC has it in the congressional record.

That's the part that should stop you for a second before we get into the broader picture.

The Council on Foreign Relations and the Congressional-Executive Commission on China both put out assessments recently, and together they document something that's been building for years: authoritarian governments have figured out that the most effective way to reach dissidents abroad isn't to send someone with a gun. It's to use the paperwork.

The two-track system the CFR lays out is worth understanding in detail. Track one is the stuff you'd expect: surveillance of diaspora communities, threats against family members still living in the home country, physical harassment, the occasional assassination of a high-profile target. Brutal, but trackable. Democratic governments have at least some tools for responding to overt violence.

Track two is where it gets genuinely difficult. Authoritarian states have learned to route their repression through legitimate international legal infrastructure. Interpol red notices. Bilateral extradition treaties. Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties, the MLAT system that's supposed to help democracies cooperate on real criminal investigations. Anti-corruption frameworks. All of it gets bent toward the same purpose: making a political dissident look like a fugitive from justice so that the host country either hands them over or has to pay a diplomatic price for refusing.

The Interpol red notice piece is particularly cynical. Interpol has done reforms. They'll say they screen for politically motivated submissions. And yet member states that have no functioning rule of law domestically continue to file notices, and the system continues to process them, because Interpol is a cooperative body and it can't function if it starts adjudicating whether member state legal systems are legitimate. Authoritarian governments know this. They file the notices. The person in Berlin or Toronto or Houston suddenly has an international flag on their name.

The anti-corruption angle is a good example of how this evolves. There's genuine international goodwill toward anti-corruption enforcement. Nobody's going to argue publicly against fighting corruption. So you take a Uyghur activist or a Hong Kong democracy organizer, and you open a corruption investigation against them back home. The charges are vague, deliberately. Political speech gets repackaged as economic crime. Now you have an "anti-corruption case" that you can present to international partners with a straight face. The target has to prove a negative in a foreign legal system, which is expensive, slow, and often impossible.

China's operation as documented by the CECC is the most extensive single-country example, but the CFR makes clear this is a multi-actor problem. What China has built is just the most systematically documented version.

The United Front Work Department coordinates political influence operations targeting diaspora community organizations. The goal is to suppress dissent, yes, but also to flip community institutions so that they become instruments of CCP political positioning rather than genuine community representation. If you control the community organization, you have eyes on who's active, who's vocal, who's organizing. That feeds the surveillance function.

The surveillance itself hits multiple layers. Social media monitoring of diaspora members. Tracking physical movements. Recruiting informants inside communities, people tasked specifically with reporting on activists, on Uyghur community members, on Tibetan advocates, on anyone connected to Hong Kong's democracy movement. The coercion mechanism that makes all of this work is the family still in China. You don't have to threaten the person in Seattle directly. You call their mother.

So what are democratic governments actually doing about this? The honest answer from both assessments is: not enough, and not coherently.

The current response is a mix of prosecuting individual cases when they surface, issuing diplomatic protests, and making policy statements. None of that adds up to a counter-architecture. It's whack-a-mole against a system that has been deliberately and patiently constructed over years.

The specific gaps the CFR identifies are worth naming. There's no comprehensive legal framework in any democratic country that specifically criminalizes acting as an agent of foreign state coercion against diaspora communities. FARA, the Foreign Agents Registration Act, is the main U.S. tool and it was designed for a different era, one where foreign agents were more or less formally identifiable. Modern transnational repression runs through informal networks and commercial entities and community organizations and family pressure. FARA doesn't fit that shape well.

Law enforcement agencies aren't sharing information about repression patterns the way they need to. If Chinese proxy operators are running the same playbook in five cities, the FBI field offices in those cities should be cross-referencing. Whether that's actually happening at the scale required is, based on these assessments, an open question with an uncomfortable implied answer.

The diplomatic reluctance piece is real and it's structural. Transnational repression is being conducted by states that are also major trade partners, debt holders, and participants in multilateral institutions that democratic governments need to function. Raising this systematically with China means raising it in a relationship where you also need cooperation on climate, on North Korea, on supply chains. That trade-off calculus doesn't make the repression acceptable, but it does explain why democratic governments keep responding case by case rather than systemically. Each individual case can be managed. A frontal policy of formally treating China's diaspora operations as a hostile intelligence campaign has consequences that foreign ministries are reluctant to invite.

The diaspora communities themselves are largely left to navigate this without adequate support infrastructure. If you're a Uyghur activist in a European city and you've received threats, or your family in Xinjiang has been contacted, who do you call? There's no dedicated mechanism. You can go to local police, who may or may not understand the transnational dimension. You can contact NGOs. What you can't do is access a government system that is specifically designed to assess your situation, document the pattern, and provide meaningful protection.

The international legal architecture gap is the deepest structural problem. There is no binding international legal framework that specifically prohibits transnational repression as a category. Individual acts might violate specific provisions of international human rights law. But the absence of a comprehensive prohibition creates exactly the ambiguity that authoritarian states exploit. They can credibly claim they're using legitimate legal processes, and until there's an international standard that defines transnational repression specifically and prohibits it, that claim is hard to defeat in international forums.

The democratic response has been primarily domestic legislation. The U.S. TRAP Act. Analogous European measures. These are real and they matter, but they're not multilateral. They don't establish binding norms. They don't create international enforcement mechanisms. An authoritarian state can note the passage of the TRAP Act and adjust its operational methods slightly. It doesn't change the underlying permissive international environment.

The CFR and CECC assessments together make a point that's uncomfortable for people who believe in the international legal order: authoritarian states are better at using that order than democracies are at defending against it. The rules-based international system has become, in part, a toolkit for repression because the rules were built assuming good-faith participants. They weren't built to handle member states that view international legal instruments as weapons to be aimed at their own citizens abroad.

Fixing that requires democracies to do something they're not historically good at: coordinating quickly across domestic and foreign policy, law enforcement and diplomacy, bilateral relationships and multilateral reform. The CECC record and the CFR analysis both suggest that the gap between the threat and the response is not closing at anything close to the right rate.

The Chinese nationals in cities across the United States who are being surveilled through those proxy stations didn't choose to be targets of a geopolitical operation. They left. That was supposed to mean something.
